title: Find the middle element of a linked list (slow/fast pointer).
shortTitle: Find the Middle Element of a Linked List — Slow/Fast Pointer

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the middle of a singly linked list uses the fast and slow pointer technique. A slow pointer advances one node at a time while a fast pointer advances two; when the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is at the middle. It finds the midpoint in a single pass, O(n) time and O(1) space, without first counting the length.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India stores a chain of transaction nodes and wants the middle transaction for a quick spot-check. Rajesh walks two fingers: one steps on every node, the other skips every other node. When the fast finger runs off the end, the slow finger is sitting right in the middle.
s1_definition.oneliner: Move one pointer by one and another by two; when the fast one finishes, the slow one is at the middle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the middle of a singly linked list uses the fast and slow pointer technique. A slow pointer advances one node at a time while a fast pointer advances two; when the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is at the middle. It finds the midpoint in a single pass, O(n) time and O(1) space, without first counting the length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India stores a chain of transaction nodes and wants the middle transaction for a quick spot-check. Rajesh walks two fingers: one steps on every node, the other skips every other node. When the fast finger runs off the end, the slow finger is sitting right in the middle.

**One line to remember:** Move one pointer by one and another by two; when the fast one finishes, the slow one is at the middle.

sections.s2_technical:
Start both `slow` and `fast` at the head. Loop while `fast != null && fast.next != null`, moving `slow = slow.next` and `fast = fast.next.next` each iteration. When the loop ends, `slow` points at the middle node. For an odd-length list the slow pointer lands exactly on the single middle; for an even-length list this formulation lands on the second of the two middle nodes.

A code snippet on a transaction list: `Node middle(Node head) { Node slow = head, fast = head; while (fast != null && fast.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; } return slow; }`. The two conditions in the while guard against a null-pointer exception: `fast != null` covers even lengths where fast steps onto null, and `fast.next != null` covers odd lengths where fast stops on the last node.

If you need the first of the two middles on an even list, start fast at `head.next` instead, or equivalently loop while `fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null`. This small change is a common interview follow-up, so knowing both variants is valuable.

The advantage over the naive two-pass method, which counts the length then walks half of it, is that this is a single pass and never needs the total length. A senior nuance is that this same slow-fast skeleton underlies cycle detection and finding a cycle's start, so recognizing the pattern connects several linked-list problems. The guard order in the while condition matters: `fast != null` must be checked before `fast.next` to avoid dereferencing null.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps the day's transactions as a singly linked list and the audit tool needs the middle transaction as a quick sampling point without scanning twice. This is exactly how the slow/fast middle finder works — one pass lands the slow pointer at the center.

Problem 2 — The list length is unknown at call time and counting it first would be a wasted extra pass over a potentially long chain, so the single-pass approach is preferred.

The code shows a `TxnListAuditor` with `middleTransaction`, a demo building a transaction list, and the middle node's id.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the odd list T1 to T5 and the even list T1 to T4.

Step 1: For the odd list, both slow and fast start at T1. Fast's next and next-next exist, so slow moves to T2 and fast jumps to T3.

Step 2: Fast at T3 still has a next and next-next, so slow moves to T3 and fast jumps to T5. Now fast is at T5 whose next is null, so the loop stops. Slow is at T3, the exact middle of five nodes.

Step 3: For the even list, slow and fast start at T1. Slow moves to T2, fast jumps to T3. Fast at T3 has a next T4, so slow moves to T3 and fast jumps to T4's next which is null.

Step 4: The loop stops because fast is null. Slow is at T3, which is the second of the two middle nodes T2 and T3 in a four-node list.

Step 5: The auditor returns T3 for the odd list and T3 for the even list, each found in a single pass without counting the length.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Middle transaction (odd length 5): T3
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Middle transaction (even length 4): T3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Odd: T1→T2→T3→T4→T5
    │ slow=T1 fast=T1
    │ slow=T2 fast=T3
    │ slow=T3 fast=T5 (fast.next null → stop)
    ▼
  Middle: T3

  Even: T1→T2→T3→T4
    │ slow=T2 fast=T3
    │ slow=T3 fast=null → stop
    ▼
  Middle: T3 (2nd middle)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the middle of a singly linked list is the classic fast-and-slow pointer problem. I start both a slow pointer and a fast pointer at the head, then advance the slow pointer one node and the fast pointer two nodes on each iteration. When the fast pointer runs off the end of the list, the slow pointer is sitting at the middle, and I have done it in a single pass without ever counting the list's length.

The guard in the loop condition is the detail I always get right. I check that the fast pointer is not null and that its next is not null before moving, and the order matters because I must confirm the fast pointer itself is non-null before I dereference its next. The first condition handles even-length lists where the fast pointer steps onto null, and the second handles odd-length lists where the fast pointer stops on the last node.

With this formulation the slow pointer lands on the single middle of an odd-length list and on the second of the two middles of an even-length list. If an interviewer asks for the first of the two middles instead, I either start the fast pointer one node ahead or loop on the fast pointer's next and next-next, which is a common follow-up worth knowing. The advantage over the naive approach of counting the length and then walking halfway is that this is a single pass that never needs the total count.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the audit tool. The day's transactions were held as a singly linked list and the tool needed the middle transaction as a quick sampling point without scanning the chain twice, and since the length was unknown at call time the single-pass slow-and-fast approach avoided a wasted counting pass over a long list. Explaining the one-and-two stepping, the null-safety guard order, and the odd-versus-even landing shows the interviewer I understand the technique that also underlies cycle detection.
